chapter.name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
chapter.blurb: The chapter describes how electrons are emitted from metals and studies the photoelectric effect experimentally: the roles of intensity, collector potential and frequency, the stopping potential and the threshold frequency. It shows why the wave theory of light cannot explain these features and how Einstein's photoelectric equation and the photon picture do. It then turns to matter and introduces de Broglie's hypothesis that a moving particle has a wavelength h/p.

scope_in.item: Recall that cathode-ray particles, particles from heated metals and from metals under ultraviolet light have the same e/m and are electrons; that Millikan's oil-drop experiment showed charge is quantised

Explain why free electrons cannot normally leave a metal, define the work function phi0 and the electron volt, convert between eV and joule, and name the three ways of electron emission (thermionic, field, photoelectric)

Describe the observations of Hertz, Hallwachs and Lenard, including the zinc-plate electroscope results and the existence of a threshold frequency that depends on the emitter material; say which metals respond to ultraviolet only and which to visible light

Describe the apparatus for studying the photoelectric effect and state how photocurrent depends on intensity and on collector potential; define saturation current and stopping potential and use Kmax = e V0 = (1/2) m vmax^2

State how the stopping potential depends on frequency (linear, zero at the threshold frequency, independent of intensity), describe the graphs in words, and list the four experimental features including instantaneous emission
Explain what the wave picture of light expects for photoelectric emission and why it fails on Kmax, threshold frequency and time lag

Use Einstein's photoelectric equation Kmax = h nu - phi0, the threshold frequency nu0 = phi0/h and e V0 = h nu - phi0 (straight line of slope h/e) in calculations, with photon energy from h nu or hc/lambda; describe Millikan's verification

State the photon picture: E = h nu = hc/lambda, p = h nu/c = h/lambda, independence of intensity, neutrality, conservation of energy and momentum but not of photon number in collisions; find the number of photons per second from N = P/E
State de Broglie's hypothesis and use lambda = h/p = h/(m v) for particles and everyday objects; show the photon satisfies it; explain why matter waves are measurable only for sub-atomic particles

concepts.name: Electron emission and the work function
concepts.description: Why free electrons stay inside a metal, the work function and the electron volt, and the three ways of supplying the energy for electron emission; the electron as a universal particle.
concepts.idea: A free electron is held inside a metal by the attraction of the ions and can come out only if it is given a certain minimum energy, the work function.
concepts.rule: Free electrons are responsible for the conductivity of a metal but cannot normally leave its surface: an electron that attempts to come out leaves the surface positively charged and is pulled back. The minimum energy required by an electron to escape from the metal surface is the work function phi0, measured in electron volt; it depends on the properties of the metal and the nature of its surface. One electron volt is the energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference of 1 volt (1 eV = 1.602 x 10^-19 J, taken as 1.6 x 10^-19 J in problems). The energy can be supplied by thermionic emission (suitable heating), field emission (a very strong electric field of the order of 10^8 V/m, as in a spark plug) or photoelectric emission (light of suitable frequency). Cathode ray particles, particles emitted by heated metals and by metals under ultraviolet light all have the same e/m (1.76 x 10^11 C/kg), independent of the material, so they are identical: electrons. Millikan's oil-drop experiment showed that charge is quantised.
concepts.example: A work function of 3.0 eV equals 3.0 x 1.6 x 10^-19 J = 4.8 x 10^-19 J.

questions.q: The minimum energy required by an electron to escape from the surface of a metal is called the
questions.a: work function of the metal

questions.a: Cooling the metal to a very low temperature

o: If an electron attempts to come out, the surface acquires a positive charge and pulls the electron back
The free electrons are fixed to individual atoms and cannot move at all
The free electrons carry no charge while they are inside the metal

questions.a: That cathode ray particles are universal, the same whatever the source

That cathode rays are electromagnetic waves and not particles
That cathode ray particles carry no mass

questions.a: electric charge is quantised

o: emission by electric discharge through a gas

questions.q: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 5 V. The energy it gains, in eV, as a whole number, is ____.
The work function of a metal is 2.5 eV. Taking 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J, its work function in joule is

The work function of a metal is 5.6 x 10^-19 J. (a) Express it in eV, taking 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J. (b) A free electron at the surface of this metal is given 2.5 eV of energy. Can it escape? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Work function = (5.6 x 10^-19 J)/(1.6 x 10^-19 J/eV) = 3.5 eV. (b) No. The electron needs at least the work function, 3.5 eV, to overcome the attractive pull of the metal, and 2.5 eV is less than this.
s: Cannot escape, because 2.5 eV is less than the work function 3.5 eV

questions.q: Metal P has a work function of 2.1 eV and metal Q has a work function of 4.3 eV. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: A free electron needs less minimum energy to come out of P than out of Q
o: A free electron needs less minimum energy to come out of P than out of Q
A free electron needs less minimum energy to come out of Q than out of P
The minimum energy needed is the same for P and Q because both are metals
No electron can ever be removed from Q, whatever energy is supplied

questions.q: An electron (charge of magnitude e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C) is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 250 V. (a) Write the energy it gains in eV. (b) Convert this energy to joule, taking 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J. (c) Is this energy larger or smaller than the work function of a metal for which the work function is 4.5 eV, and by what factor (to 2 significant figures)?
questions.a: (a) An electron accelerated through 1 V gains 1 eV, so through 250 V it gains 250 eV. (b) Energy = 250 x 1.6 x 10^-19 J = 4.0 x 10^-17 J. (c) It is larger than the work function: 250 eV / 4.5 eV = 55.6, that is about 56 times the work function.
s: Energy gained = 250 eV
Larger than 4.5 eV, by a factor of about 56

questions.q: Assertion (A): Certain metals emit electrons when they are heated to a high temperature. Reason (R): Suitable heating imparts sufficient thermal energy to the free electrons to enable them to come out of the metal. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: Thermionic emission, field emission and photoelectric emission are three different processes. State what is common to all three as far as a free electron in the metal is concerned, and what is different.
questions.a: Common: in each case the free electron is supplied with at least the minimum energy (the work function) that it needs to overcome the attractive pull of the metal and come out of the surface. Different: the agency that supplies this energy - heat in thermionic emission, a very strong electric field in field emission, and light of suitable frequency in photoelectric emission.
s: Common - each supplies the electron with at least the work function so that it can overcome the attractive pull
Different - the source of the energy: heating, strong electric field, light of suitable frequency

questions.q: Two metals A and B have work functions 2.0 eV and 5.0 eV respectively. A free electron at the surface of each metal is supplied with 6.4 x 10^-19 J of energy. Taking 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J, convert the supplied energy to eV and decide, with reasons, for which metal the electron can come out.
questions.a: Supplied energy = (6.4 x 10^-19 J)/(1.6 x 10^-19 J/eV) = 4.0 eV. For metal A the work function is 2.0 eV, which is less than 4.0 eV, so the electron has more than the minimum energy needed and can come out. For metal B the work function is 5.0 eV, which is more than 4.0 eV, so the electron cannot overcome the attractive pull and stays inside the metal.
s: Supplied energy = 4.0 eV
Metal A: 4.0 eV exceeds 2.0 eV, electron can escape
Metal B: 4.0 eV is less than 5.0 eV, electron cannot escape

questions.q: A student says: 'The conduction electrons of a metal are called free electrons, so they are free to leave the metal whenever they like.' Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is wrong. The electrons are free only in the sense that they can move about inside the metal, which is why the metal conducts. They are held inside the surface by the attractive forces of the ions: an electron trying to leave is pulled back. It can come out only if it is given a certain minimum energy, the work function of the metal.
s: Judgement - wrong: free to move inside the metal, not free to leave it
Reason - held by the attraction of the ions; needs at least the work function to escape

questions.q: Write a short explanatory note for a classmate on the term 'work function'. Your note must (a) say what it is, (b) give its symbol, its usual unit and what it depends on, and (c) include one numerical illustration of your own that converts a work function from eV to joule using 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J.
questions.a: (a) The work function is the minimum energy required by an electron to escape from the surface of a metal. (b) It is denoted by phi0, is usually measured in electron volt (eV), and depends on the properties of the metal and the nature of its surface. (c) Illustration (any correct one earns the mark): a metal with phi0 = 4.0 eV has phi0 = 4.0 x 1.6 x 10^-19 J = 6.4 x 10^-19 J.
s: Correct meaning - minimum energy for an electron to escape from the metal surface
Symbol phi0, unit eV, depends on the metal and the nature of its surface
A correct eV-to-joule illustration of the student's own

concepts.name: Discovery of the photoelectric effect: Hertz, Hallwachs and Lenard
concepts.description: The early observations of photoelectric emission, the threshold frequency as an experimental fact, and which metals respond to ultraviolet or to visible light.
concepts.idea: Light of suitable frequency falling on a metal makes it emit electrons (photoelectrons), and no emission occurs below a minimum frequency that depends on the metal.
concepts.rule: Hertz (1887) found that sparks across his detector loop were enhanced when the emitter plate was illuminated by ultraviolet light. Lenard found that ultraviolet radiation falling on the emitter plate of an evacuated tube with two electrodes gives a current in the circuit, which stops as soon as the radiation is stopped: electrons ejected from emitter C are attracted to the positive collector A. Hallwachs (1888) found that a negatively charged zinc plate loses its charge under ultraviolet light, an uncharged zinc plate becomes positively charged, and a positively charged plate becomes more positive, so negatively charged particles are emitted. After the electron was discovered in 1897 these were recognised as electrons and called photoelectrons. No electrons are emitted when the frequency of the light is below a certain minimum value, the threshold frequency, which depends on the emitter material. Zinc, cadmium and magnesium respond only to ultraviolet light; alkali metals such as lithium, sodium, potassium, caesium and rubidium respond even to visible light.
concepts.example: In Lenard's evacuated tube a current flowed while ultraviolet light fell on the emitter plate and stopped as soon as the light was cut off.

questions.q: The phenomenon of photoelectric emission was discovered in 1887 by
questions.a: Heinrich Hertz

questions.q: The electrons emitted from a metal surface when light of suitable frequency illuminates it are called ____ (write one word, in the plural).
questions.a: photoelectrons

questions.q: In Hallwachs' study of 1888, the metal plate that was connected to an electroscope and illuminated by ultraviolet light was made of

The observations were made with ultraviolet radiation

questions.a: It depends on the nature of the emitter material and is lower for the alkali metals

be emitted, because the light is very bright
be emitted after a delay of a few minutes
be emitted only if the red light is made dimmer

questions.a: The positive charge on the plate is further enhanced (it increases). Ultraviolet light makes the zinc plate emit negatively charged particles (electrons); losing negative charge leaves the plate with a larger net positive charge.

questions.a: Caesium

questions.q: In Lenard's experiment the two metal plates were enclosed in an evacuated glass tube. Which observation showed that the current was carried by particles ejected from the emitter and not by the gas in the tube?
questions.a: Current flowed although the tube was evacuated, and stopped as soon as the ultraviolet light was cut off
o: Current flowed although the tube was evacuated, and stopped as soon as the ultraviolet light was cut off

questions.q: Three light sources of frequencies 4.0 x 10^14 Hz, 6.0 x 10^14 Hz and 9.0 x 10^14 Hz are available, and two emitter plates: X with threshold frequency 5.0 x 10^14 Hz and Y with threshold frequency 8.0 x 10^14 Hz. (a) Which sources give photoelectric emission from X? (b) Which sources give emission from Y? (c) The 4.0 x 10^14 Hz source is made ten times more intense. Does it now give emission from X? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Emission needs a frequency not smaller than the threshold frequency. For X (5.0 x 10^14 Hz) the 6.0 x 10^14 Hz and 9.0 x 10^14 Hz sources give emission; the 4.0 x 10^14 Hz source does not. (b) For Y (8.0 x 10^14 Hz) only the 9.0 x 10^14 Hz source gives emission. (c) No. 4.0 x 10^14 Hz is still below the threshold frequency of X, and below the threshold frequency no electrons are emitted at all, however intense the light.
s: X: 6.0 x 10^14 Hz and 9.0 x 10^14 Hz sources only
Y: 9.0 x 10^14 Hz source only
No emission - frequency still below threshold; intensity does not matter

questions.q: (I) Hallwachs and Lenard observed that when the frequency of the light falling on the emitter plate was smaller than a certain minimum value, no electrons were emitted at all. (II) This minimum frequency has the same value for every emitter material. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: Hertz observed the effect of ultraviolet light on his spark gap in 1887, but the particles involved could be clearly identified only after 1897. Explain what happened in 1897 and how it changed the interpretation of the observations of Hertz, Hallwachs and Lenard.
questions.a: In 1897 the electron was discovered (by J. J. Thomson). After this it became evident that the incident light causes electrons to be emitted from the emitter plate: the 'negatively charged particles' of the earlier observations were electrons, and they came to be called photoelectrons and the phenomenon the photoelectric effect.
s: 1897 - discovery of the electron
The emitted negative particles were identified as electrons (photoelectrons) ejected by the light

questions.q: Using only Hallwachs' electroscope observations on a zinc plate illuminated by ultraviolet light, argue that the particles emitted by the plate carry negative and not positive charge. Use the behaviour of the plate when it starts negatively charged, uncharged and positively charged.
questions.a: A negatively charged plate loses its charge under ultraviolet light, which is what happens if negative charge leaves it. An uncharged plate becomes positively charged, which again means negative charge has left it. The charge of a positively charged plate is further enhanced, again because negative charge leaves. If the emitted particles were positive, the uncharged plate would have become negative and the positive plate would have lost charge. All three observations are consistent only with the emission of negatively charged particles.
s: Negative plate loses its charge - negative charge leaving
Uncharged plate becomes positive and positive plate becomes more positive
Argument - emission of positive particles would give the opposite results, so the particles are negative

questions.q: A student claims: 'Any metal will emit electrons under any kind of light, provided the light is bright enough.' Evaluate this claim using the findings of Hallwachs and Lenard.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. Hallwachs and Lenard found that no electrons are emitted at all when the frequency of the incident light is smaller than a certain minimum value, the threshold frequency, which depends on the emitter material. So a metal such as zinc, which responds only to ultraviolet light, emits nothing under visible light however bright it is.
s: Judgement - wrong; emission needs a frequency at or above the threshold frequency of the material
Support - e.g. zinc responds only to ultraviolet; brightness cannot make up for low frequency

questions.q: Design a demonstration, using a zinc plate, an electroscope, an ultraviolet lamp and an ordinary visible-light lamp, to show that ultraviolet light makes zinc emit negative charge. Describe the procedure, a control, and the expected observations.
questions.a: Procedure: connect the clean zinc plate to the electroscope and give it a negative charge so that the leaves diverge; then shine the ultraviolet lamp on the plate. Expected: the leaves collapse, showing that the plate loses its negative charge. Control: recharge the plate negatively and shine the visible-light lamp on it instead; the leaves stay diverged, because zinc responds only to ultraviolet light. Conclusion: ultraviolet light makes the zinc plate emit negatively charged particles (electrons).
s: Procedure - negatively charged zinc plate on an electroscope, illuminated with ultraviolet light
Observation - leaves collapse / plate loses its negative charge
Control with visible light shows no discharge, and conclusion that negative particles are emitted

concepts.name: Experimental study of the photoelectric effect
concepts.description: The apparatus and the dependence of photocurrent on intensity and collector potential; saturation current, stopping potential and its dependence on frequency; the four experimental features.
concepts.idea: Intensity controls how many photoelectrons are emitted per second, while frequency controls how energetic the most energetic of them are.
concepts.rule: Apparatus: evacuated tube with photosensitive emitter C and collector A, quartz window, battery with commutator, voltmeter and microammeter; frequency is changed with coloured filters and intensity by changing the distance of the source. (i) For a given material and frequency above threshold, photocurrent is directly proportional to intensity. (ii) As the collector is made more positive the current rises to a maximum, the saturation current, when all emitted electrons are collected; saturation current is proportional to intensity. With a retarding potential the current falls to zero at the stopping (cut-off) potential V0, and Kmax = e V0 = (1/2) m vmax^2. For a given frequency V0 is independent of intensity. (iii) For the same intensity, a higher frequency gives a larger stopping potential but the same saturation current; V0 varies linearly with frequency and is zero at the threshold frequency nu0, below which there is no emission however intense the light. (iv) Emission is instantaneous (about 10^-9 s or less) even for very dim light.
concepts.example: If the photocurrent stops at a retarding potential of 0.60 V, the most energetic photoelectrons have Kmax = 0.60 eV.

questions.q: In the arrangement used for the experimental study of the photoelectric effect, the photocurrent in the circuit is measured by a
questions.a: microammeter

questions.q: The maximum value of the photoelectric current, beyond which a further increase of the collector's positive potential produces no further increase, is called the ____ current (write one word).

questions.q: For a particular frequency of incident radiation, the minimum negative (retarding) potential given to the collector plate for which the photocurrent becomes zero is called the
questions.a: cut-off or stopping potential

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a correct experimental feature of the photoelectric effect?
questions.a: For light of a given frequency, the stopping potential increases when the intensity is increased
o: For light of a given frequency, the stopping potential increases when the intensity is increased
For a given frequency above the threshold, the photocurrent increases when the intensity is increased
Emission begins without any apparent time lag (about 10^-9 s or less), even for very dim light
Above the threshold frequency, the stopping potential increases linearly with frequency

questions.q: With the frequency of the light and the collector potential kept fixed, the photocurrent is found to increase linearly with the intensity of the light. This implies that
questions.a: the number of photoelectrons emitted per second is directly proportional to the intensity
o: the number of photoelectrons emitted per second is directly proportional to the intensity
the energy of each photoelectron is directly proportional to the intensity
the threshold frequency falls as the intensity rises
the speed of each photoelectron doubles when the intensity doubles

questions.q: As the accelerating (positive) potential of the collector is increased, the photocurrent first rises and then stops rising. Why does it stop rising?
questions.a: All the photoelectrons emitted by the emitter are already reaching the collector
o: All the photoelectrons emitted by the emitter are already reaching the collector
The emitter stops emitting photoelectrons at high potential
The collector begins to repel the photoelectrons
The light can no longer reach the emitter

questions.q: A quartz window is sealed on to the tube used for studying the photoelectric effect because quartz
questions.a: lets ultraviolet radiation pass through to the photosensitive plate
o: lets ultraviolet radiation pass through to the photosensitive plate
blocks ultraviolet radiation from reaching the plate
emits photoelectrons more readily than metals
measures the intensity of the incident light

questions.q: When the collector is at the stopping potential, the photocurrent is zero because
questions.a: even the most energetic photoelectrons are repelled before they reach the collector
o: even the most energetic photoelectrons are repelled before they reach the collector
all the photoelectrons are emitted with zero kinetic energy
the incident light is reflected back by the collector

questions.q: Radiation of the same intensity but of three different frequencies nu1 < nu2 < nu3 (all above the threshold) is used in turn on the same emitter. The three curves of photocurrent against collector potential show
questions.a: different stopping potentials but the same saturation current
o: different stopping potentials but the same saturation current
the same stopping potential but different saturation currents
different stopping potentials and different saturation currents
the same stopping potential and the same saturation current

questions.q: In a photoelectric experiment the stopping potential is 2.5 V. The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, in eV, as a decimal, is ____.

For a given emitter and light of a fixed frequency above the threshold, the saturation current is 4 microampere. If the intensity of the light is doubled at the same frequency, the saturation current becomes
questions.a: 8 microampere

questions.q: The stopping potential in a photoelectric experiment is 2.0 V. Taking e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons in joule is

Light of frequency nu1 (above threshold) gives a saturation current of 6 microampere. The frequency is raised to nu2 > nu1 and the intensity adjusted to the same value as before. The saturation current is now
questions.a: 6 microampere

questions.q: For a certain metal the graph of stopping potential against frequency of the incident radiation is a straight line that meets the frequency axis at 5.0 x 10^14 Hz. (a) What is this frequency called? (b) What is observed when very intense light of frequency 4.0 x 10^14 Hz falls on the metal?
questions.a: (a) It is the threshold (cut-off) frequency of the metal, the frequency at which the stopping potential is zero. (b) No photoelectric emission takes place: 4.0 x 10^14 Hz is lower than the threshold frequency, and below it no photoelectrons are emitted however large the intensity.
s: Threshold (cut-off) frequency
No emission, since the frequency is below threshold whatever the intensity

questions.q: In a photoelectric experiment the photocurrent falls to zero when the collector is at 1.8 V negative with respect to the emitter. Take e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C and the electron mass m = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons (a) in eV and (b) in joule, and (c) their maximum speed, to 2 significant figures.
questions.a: (a) Kmax = e V0 = 1.8 eV. (b) Kmax = 1.6 x 10^-19 C x 1.8 V = 2.88 x 10^-19 J. (c) Kmax = (1/2) m vmax^2, so vmax = sqrt(2 Kmax/m) = sqrt(2 x 2.88 x 10^-19 / 9.11 x 10^-31) = sqrt(6.32 x 10^11) m/s = 8.0 x 10^5 m/s (to 2 significant figures).
s: Kmax = e V0 = 1.8 eV
vmax = sqrt(2 Kmax/m) = 8.0 x 10^5 m/s

questions.q: Assertion (A): When the incident radiation has a frequency above the threshold frequency, photoelectric emission starts without any apparent time lag even if the radiation is very dim. Reason (R): For a given photosensitive material and frequency of incident radiation, the saturation current does not depend on the intensity of the radiation. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, R is false

concepts.name: Failure of the wave theory and Einstein's photoelectric equation
concepts.description: What the wave picture of light predicts for photoelectric emission and why it fails; Einstein's light quanta, the photoelectric equation, threshold frequency and the stopping potential versus frequency line; Millikan's verification.
concepts.idea: One electron absorbs one quantum of energy h nu; part of it is used to leave the metal and the rest appears as kinetic energy.
concepts.rule: Wave picture: energy is absorbed continuously, so Kmax should rise with intensity, no threshold frequency should exist, and in dim light an electron could need hours to gather enough energy; all three contradict observation. Einstein (1905): radiation consists of quanta of energy h nu, and an electron absorbs one quantum. Kmax = h nu - phi0. Emission is possible only if h nu > phi0, so the threshold frequency is nu0 = phi0/h; a larger work function means a higher threshold frequency. Intensity is proportional to the number of quanta per unit area per unit time, so it fixes the number of electrons emitted (the photocurrent), not Kmax. Absorption of a quantum is instantaneous, so there is no time lag. With Kmax = e V0: e V0 = h nu - phi0, or V0 = (h/e) nu - phi0/e, a straight line of slope h/e that is the same for all materials. Millikan (1906-1916) measured this slope for sodium, obtained h close to 6.626 x 10^-34 J s and so verified the equation. In problems h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s and e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C.
concepts.example: Caesium has work function 2.14 eV, so its threshold frequency is (2.14 x 1.6 x 10^-19 J)/(6.63 x 10^-34 J s) = 5.16 x 10^14 Hz.

questions.q: The wave picture of light fails to explain three basic features of photoelectric emission. For each of these three features, state what the wave picture expects and how Einstein's picture of light quanta accounts for what is actually observed.
questions.a: (1) Maximum kinetic energy: the wave picture expects it to increase with intensity, since a more intense wave gives more energy to each electron. Observed: it is independent of intensity. Einstein: one electron absorbs one quantum h nu, so Kmax = h nu - phi0 depends on frequency only. (2) Threshold frequency: the wave picture expects that a sufficiently intense beam of any frequency can eject electrons, so no threshold should exist. Einstein: emission needs h nu greater than phi0, so there is a threshold frequency nu0 = phi0/h. (3) Time lag: with continuous absorption spread over the wavefront, an electron could need hours to gather enough energy. Observed: emission is instantaneous. Einstein: absorption of a quantum by an electron is an instantaneous process whatever the intensity.
s: Kmax - wave picture: grows with intensity; Einstein: Kmax = h nu - phi0, set by the quantum energy
Threshold - wave picture: none expected; Einstein: needs h nu > phi0, so nu0 = phi0/h
Time lag - wave picture: long delay in dim light; Einstein: absorption of one quantum is instantaneous

questions.q: A student argues: 'A very dim ultraviolet beam delivers little energy per second, so the electrons in the metal must wait and collect energy before any of them can be emitted.' Evaluate this argument using Einstein's picture, assuming the frequency is above the threshold.
questions.a: The argument is the wave picture and is wrong. In Einstein's picture an electron does not collect energy gradually; it absorbs a single quantum of energy h nu in one instantaneous process, and since h nu exceeds the work function it is emitted at once. A dim beam simply has fewer quanta per second, so fewer electrons are emitted per second (smaller photocurrent), but there is no delay.
s: Judgement - wrong: emission is by absorption of a single quantum, which is instantaneous
Dim beam means fewer quanta per second, so a smaller current but no delay

questions.a: One possible design: choose wavelength 496 nm, which lies between 400 nm and 620 nm. Photon energy = 1240 eV nm / 496 nm = 2.5 eV. For a stopping potential of 1.0 V we need Kmax = 1.0 eV, so the work function must be phi0 = 2.5 eV - 1.0 eV = 1.5 eV. Check: Kmax = h nu - phi0 = 2.5 - 1.5 = 1.0 eV, so V0 = Kmax/e = 1.0 V. (Any wavelength in the range with phi0 = photon energy - 1.0 eV is acceptable.)
s: A wavelength in the range chosen and its photon energy found from 1240/lambda
Work function chosen as photon energy minus 1.0 eV
Check with Kmax = h nu - phi0 and e V0 = Kmax giving 1.0 V

concepts.name: Particle nature of light: the photon
concepts.description: The photon picture of electromagnetic radiation: energy and momentum of a photon, independence of intensity, neutrality, conservation in collisions, and counting photons in a beam of given power.
concepts.idea: In its interaction with matter, radiation behaves as if made of particles called photons, each with a definite energy and momentum.
concepts.rule: Each photon has energy E = h nu = hc/lambda, momentum p = h nu/c = h/lambda and speed c. All photons of light of a particular frequency have the same energy and momentum whatever the intensity; increasing the intensity only increases the number of photons per second crossing a given area. Photons are electrically neutral and are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields. In a photon-particle collision total energy and total momentum are conserved, but the number of photons need not be: a photon may be absorbed or a new one created. A source of power P emitting photons of energy E emits N = P/E photons per second. Compton's experiment (1924) on scattering of X-rays from electrons further confirmed the particle-like behaviour. Which description, wave or particle, suits an experiment depends on the experiment.
concepts.example: Light of frequency 6.0 x 10^14 Hz has photons of energy 6.63 x 10^-34 x 6.0 x 10^14 = 3.98 x 10^-19 J; a 2.0 x 10^-3 W source of it emits 5.0 x 10^15 photons per second.

concepts.name: Wave nature of matter: the de Broglie wavelength
concepts.description: De Broglie's hypothesis that moving particles have a wavelength h/p, its consistency for the photon, and why it matters only for sub-atomic particles.
concepts.idea: A moving particle of momentum p has an associated matter wave of wavelength h/p, which is noticeable only when the momentum is extremely small.
concepts.rule: De Broglie (1924) reasoned that nature is symmetrical: if radiation has a dual nature, so should matter. The de Broglie wavelength is lambda = h/p = h/(m v). The relation joins a wave attribute (lambda) with a particle attribute (p) through Planck's constant. For a material particle it is a hypothesis to be tested by experiment; for a photon, p = h nu/c gives h/p = c/nu, the wavelength of the radiation, so the photon satisfies it too. lambda is smaller for a heavier or faster particle and does not depend on the charge or nature of the particle. For macroscopic objects it is far too small to measure; for sub-atomic particles such as electrons and protons it is of the order of the spacing of atomic planes in crystals and is measurable.
concepts.example: A ball of mass 0.12 kg moving at 20 m/s has p = 2.40 kg m/s and lambda = 6.63 x 10^-34 / 2.40 = 2.76 x 10^-34 m.

(b) Find, to 2 significant figures, the de Broglie wavelength of an electron (mass 9.11 x 10^-31 kg) moving at 7.28 x 10^6 m/s. (c) State which of the two wavelengths could be measured, and why.

(b) p = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg x 7.28 x 10^6 m/s = 6.63 x 10^-24 kg m/s, so lambda = 6.63 x 10^-34 / 6.63 x 10^-24 = 1.0 x 10^-10 m (0.10 nm). (c) Only the electron's: 10^-10 m is of the order of the spacing of atomic planes in crystals (comparable with X-ray wavelengths), whereas the bullet's 5.0 x 10^-35 m is far too small for any measurement.

Electron: p = 6.63 x 10^-24 kg m/s, lambda = 1.0 x 10^-10 m

questions.q: Show that the wavelength of electromagnetic radiation is equal to the de Broglie wavelength of its quantum, the photon. Then state what this result says about the de Broglie relation.
questions.a: A photon of radiation of frequency nu has momentum p = h nu/c. Its de Broglie wavelength is therefore h/p = h/(h nu/c) = c/nu. But c/nu is the wavelength lambda of the electromagnetic radiation of frequency nu. So the de Broglie wavelength of the photon equals the wavelength of the radiation of which it is the quantum. This shows that the de Broglie relation, proposed as a hypothesis for material particles, is also satisfied by the photon.
s: Photon momentum p = h nu/c

c/nu is the wavelength of the radiation, so the relation is satisfied by the photon as well

questions.q: A student says: 'A cricket ball has far more momentum than an electron, so its wave nature should be far easier to observe.' Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is wrong. The de Broglie wavelength is lambda = h/p, so a larger momentum gives a smaller wavelength. questions.q: Construct two examples of your own, one sub-atomic particle and one everyday object, choosing a mass and a speed for each. Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of each using h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s, and use your results to explain where the wave character of matter is significant.
questions.a: One possible answer: a proton of mass 1.67 x 10^-27 kg moving at 1.0 x 10^4 m/s has p = 1.67 x 10^-23 kg m/s and lambda = 6.63 x 10^-34 / 1.67 x 10^-23 = 4.0 x 10^-11 m. A ball of mass 0.50 kg moving at 10 m/s has p = 5.0 kg m/s and lambda = 6.63 x 10^-34 / 5.0 = 1.3 x 10^-34 m. The proton's wavelength is comparable with atomic dimensions and is measurable, whereas the ball's is far beyond measurement. So the wave character is significant only in the sub-atomic domain, where masses and momenta are very small.
